messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Tariq is a 54-year-old community organizer, married, who came to therapy at his wife's urging after months of withdrawal and what she described as a "shadow" settling over him. The event that shattered his life happened two years ago, in his own home, at the hands of his then-partner — a man he had loved and trusted for years. It began with an argument over something trivial, but quickly escalated. Tariq remembers being pushed against the kitchen counter, then struck across the face with a closed fist. The next few minutes are not a continuous memory but a series of fragments: the sound of his own head hitting the tile floor, the weight of a knee on his chest, the roar of a helicopter passing low overhead that seemed to drown out his own voice pleading for it to stop. He did not call the police. He did not tell anyone for months. He was certain that he had somehow brought this on himself — that the event happened to him because of the sort of person he is, weak and deserving of punishment. This belief in his own fundamental flaw has only deepened over time.

What Tariq did not anticipate was how the world would begin to feel like a landscape of hidden threats. He had always been an outgoing man, comfortable in crowds and public spaces, but now he finds himself scanning every room he enters, watching for people who might be dangerous. This hypervigilance is exhausting, but he cannot stop. It is triggered most powerfully by darkness: walking into a dim hallway or a parking garage at night instantly brings back the fragmented memory, the sound of the helicopter, the helplessness. He has come to avoid the site of the assault entirely — a neighborhood coffee shop he used to love — because even passing it on the bus can bring the memory flooding back without warning. Increasingly, he wears concealing clothing: oversized jackets and baseball caps pulled low, hoping to become invisible, to not be noticed or targeted. But these strategies only reinforce his belief that he is fundamentally marked, that he was betrayed because he is weak. The more he hides, the more he feels that the world is full of people who could hurt him.

The causal loop has tightened around him. A single trigger — a dark street, a distant helicopter sound — can pull him into a fragmented, auditory memory that feels as real as the event itself. That memory then confirms his belief that he is a certain kind of person, someone who invites betrayal, and this appraisal makes him more sensitive to triggers, more vigilant, more avoidant. His avoidance of the event site and his hypervigilance toward people have not protected him; they have only narrowed his world and deepened his shame. At work, he has stopped attending evening community meetings, citing vague health reasons, and his colleagues have noticed. His wife has found him standing in the dark hallway of their apartment, frozen, listening to nothing. What finally brought him to seek help was a moment two weeks ago when he saw a man who vaguely resembled his ex-partner at a grocery store, and Tariq found himself unable to breathe, the memory of the helicopter sound roaring in his ears. He is afraid of what he might do if he keeps going this way — afraid that his own mind has become a place he cannot escape. But he is also, quietly, hoping that someone can help him understand why he cannot stop believing that he deserved it.
